---
title: '<span class="discogenic-pain-module-title">Discogenic Pain</span><span class="discogenic-pain-subsection-title">Management</span>'
---

Discogenic pain is managed along a stepwise ladder, beginning with conservative and pharmacologic care, escalating to interventional procedures for refractory cases, and reserving surgery for a carefully selected minority. Because most axial back pain improves over time and no imaging finding reliably confirms a painful disc, treatment prioritizes function over cure, and invasive options are used only after conservative care fails.

## Conservative Care

- **Education and activity:** Reassure the patient, discourage bed rest, and encourage early return to normal activity with realistic expectations for gradual recovery.
- **Exercise therapy:** The cornerstone of care; supervised, individualized programs focused on core stabilization, stretching, and general strengthening.
- **Psychological and multidisciplinary care:** CBT and multidisciplinary biopsychosocial rehabilitation for chronic, disabling pain.

## Pharmacologic Therapy

- NSAIDs for short-term pain relief.
- Duloxetine for chronic pain, particularly when NSAIDs are inadequate or contraindicated.
- **Avoid:** Acetaminophen (ineffective for low back pain), benzodiazepines, systemic corticosteroids, and long-term opioids, which carry substantial risk with little sustained benefit.

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea

There is no drug that reverses disc degeneration. Pharmacotherapy aims only to reduce pain enough to enable exercise and function.
:::

## Procedural and Surgical Interventions

::: {.disc-management-table}
| Intervention | Description | Role |
|-|-|-|
| **Basivertebral nerve ablation (BVNA)** | Probe advanced transpedicularly into the vertebral body; radiofrequency ablates the basivertebral nerve | Interrupts endplate pain signals in the vertebrogenic subtype |
| **Intradiscal biologics (PRP, stem cells)** | Injection of platelet-rich plasma or stem cells into the disc | Emerging therapy that may improve pain and function in selected patients; evidence remains limited |
| **Epidural steroid injection** | Corticosteroid into the epidural space | Reduces perineural inflammation (radicular, not axial, pain) |
| **Lumbar fusion** | Removal of symptomatic disc and rigid fixation of adjacent vertebrae | Eliminates motion at the painful segment |
| **Total disc replacement** | Excision of disc and insertion of a mobile prosthesis | Removes painful disc while preserving segmental motion |
:::
